html:
Nixtamalisation is the Mesoamerican way of preparing maize: the grain is soaked and cooked in water with lime or wood ash, then washed and hulled. It was in use in Mexico and Central America by about 1500 BCE, and it is still how tortillas and tamales are made.

The alkaline bath does several things at once. It loosens the tough hulls and softens the kernels, so they grind easily. It lets the ground maize form a dough, called masa; untreated cornmeal will not hold together. It improves taste and smell, and it destroys most of the toxins left by moulds. Most important, it frees niacin (vitamin B3) in a form the body can use.

That last point mattered across history. Peoples who lived on maize with this process, from the Olmecs to the Maya and the Aztecs, stayed healthy on it. When maize spread to Europe, Africa and Asia in the Columbian Exchange, the crop travelled but the technique did not. Poor farmers in places like northern Italy who ate mostly maize fell ill with pellagra, a niacin deficiency disease, in the 1700s and 1800s (see maize in Venetia). Only later did science explain what Mesoamerican cooks had known for three thousand years.
